segments.title: Experience and better programmed decisions
segments.script: Managers can use a variety of techniques to improve their decision-making by making better-quality decisions or making decisions more quickly. An often overlooked factor in effective decision-making is experience. Managers with more experience have generally learned more and developed greater expertise that they can draw on when making decisions. Experience helps managers develop methods and heuristics to quickly deal with programmed decisions and helps them know what additional information to seek out before making a nonprogrammed decision. In addition, experience enables managers to recognize when to minimize the time spent making decisions on issues that are not particularly important but must still be addressed. As discussed previously, heuristics are mental shortcuts that managers take when making programmed (routine, low-involvement) decisions. Another technique that managers use with these types of decisions is satisficing. When satisficing, a decision maker selects the first acceptable solution without engaging in additional effort to identify the best solution. We all engage in satisficing every day. For example, suppose you are shopping for groceries and you don't want to overspend. If you have plenty of time, you might compare prices and figure out the price by weight (or volume) to ensure that every item you select is the cheapest option. But if you are in a hurry, you might just select generic products, knowing that they are cheap enough. This allows you to finish the task quickly at a reasonably low cost.
keyPoints: Experience helps managers build heuristics for programmed decisions and know what information to seek for nonprogrammed ones
Satisficing means picking the first acceptable option instead of searching for the best one
Satisficing saves time and works well for low-stakes, routine choices, like a quick grocery trip
Managers use heuristics and satisficing together to move quickly through decisions that do not need deep analysis
segments.altExplanation: Satisficing means settling for good enough rather than searching for the perfect option. It pairs naturally with heuristics: both are timesaving shortcuts suited to decisions that are not worth a lot of deliberation. Experience makes both sharper, because a manager who has seen a problem before recognizes it faster.
segments.deeper: Satisficing connects to bounded rationality from earlier in the chapter: because managers cannot process every alternative, settling for the first acceptable option is often the rational response to that limit, not a shortcut to be ashamed of. The chapter treats experience as a compounding advantage, since it sharpens the heuristics used for programmed decisions and tells a manager what information is worth chasing before tackling a nonprogrammed one.

checkpoint.prompt: Explain what satisficing is and when it may be a good strategy.
checkpoint.answer: Satisficing means selecting the first acceptable solution instead of searching for the best possible one. It is a good strategy for programmed, low-stakes decisions where speed matters more than optimizing every detail, such as quickly picking a good-enough grocery item instead of comparing every price.
checkpoint.rubric: Must define satisficing as choosing the first acceptable option rather than the optimal one, and say it fits routine or programmed, low-stakes decisions where time matters more than finding the best option. A bare 'it saves time' without the definition is not enough.

checkpoint.prompt: According to the passage, what does experience help a manager do before making a nonprogrammed decision?
options: Rely only on heuristics instead of research
Skip the decision-making process entirely
Know what additional information to seek out
Avoid ever consulting other people
checkpoint.answer: Know what additional information to seek out
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about knowing what additional information to seek out.

segments.title: Recognizing problems, generating alternatives
segments.script: For situations in which the quality of the decision is more critical than the time spent on the decision, decision makers can use several tactics. As stated previously, nonprogrammed decisions should be addressed using a systematic process. We therefore discuss these tactics within the context of the decision-making steps. To review, the steps include the following: Recognize that a decision needs to be made. Generate multiple alternatives. Analyze the alternatives. Select an alternative. Implement the selected alternative. Evaluate its effectiveness. Step 1: Recognizing That a Decision Needs to Be Made Ineffective managers will sometimes ignore problems because they aren't sure how to address them. However, this tends to lead to more and bigger problems over time. Effective managers will be attentive to problems and to opportunities and will not shy away from making decisions that could make their team, department, or organization more effective and more successful. Step 2: Generating Multiple Alternatives Often a manager only spends enough time on Step 2 to generate two alternatives and then quickly moves to Step 3 in order to make a quick decision. A better solution may have been available, but it wasn't even considered. It's important to remember that for nonprogrammed decisions, you don't want to rush the process. Generating many possible options will increase the likelihood of reaching a good decision. Some tactics to help with generating more options include talking to other people (to get their ideas) and thinking creatively about the problem.
keyPoints: Nonprogrammed decisions should follow a systematic six-step process rather than being made quickly
Step 1 is recognizing that a decision needs to be made; ignoring problems lets them grow bigger over time
Step 2 is generating multiple alternatives; managers often stop at just two options and move on too fast
Generating many options, rather than settling early, increases the likelihood of reaching a good decision
segments.altExplanation: Skipping steps is the main way nonprogrammed decisions go wrong. The passage flags two early traps: managers who avoid recognizing a problem at all, and managers who stop generating options after just two. Both trade thoroughness for speed on a decision that was supposed to get careful treatment.
segments.deeper: This six-step process is the nonprogrammed decision-making process introduced earlier in the chapter; here the book walks through what good execution of each step looks like. The warning about generating only two alternatives connects to bounded rationality: managers naturally want to economize on effort, but nonprogrammed decisions are exactly the cases where that shortcut can cost the most.

checkpoint.prompt: What are the six steps in the decision-making process?
checkpoint.answer: The six steps are: recognize that a decision needs to be made, generate multiple alternatives, analyze the alternatives, select an alternative, implement the selected alternative, and evaluate its effectiveness.
checkpoint.rubric: Must list at least five of the six steps in roughly the right order: recognize the need for a decision, generate alternatives, analyze alternatives, select an alternative, implement it, evaluate its effectiveness.

checkpoint.prompt: Why do ineffective managers let problems grow bigger, according to the passage?
options: They evaluate their decisions too many times
They generate too many alternatives to choose from
They talk to too many other people first
They ignore problems they don't know how to fix
checkpoint.answer: They ignore problems they don't know how to fix
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about ignoring problems out of uncertainty over how to address them.

segments.title: Talking to others and being creative
segments.script: Managers can often improve the quality of their decision-making by involving others in the process, especially when generating alternatives. Other people tend to view problems from different perspectives because they have had different life experiences. This can help generate alternatives that you might not otherwise have considered. Talking through big decisions with a mentor can also be beneficial, especially for new managers who are still learning and developing their expertise; someone with more experience will often be able to suggest more options. We don't always associate management with creativity, but creativity can be quite beneficial in some situations. In decision-making, creativity can be particularly helpful when generating alternatives. Creativity is the generation of new or original ideas; it requires the use of imagination and the ability to step back from traditional ways of doing things and seeing the world. While some people seem to be naturally creative, it is a skill that you can develop. Being creative requires letting your mind wander and combining existing knowledge from past experiences in novel ways. Creative inspiration may come when we least expect it (in the shower, for example) because we aren't intensely focused on the problem, we've allowed our minds to wander. Managers who strive to be creative will take the time to view a problem from multiple perspectives, try to combine information in news ways, search for overarching patterns, and use their imaginations to generate new solutions to existing problems. We'll review creativity in more detail in Chapter 18. Step 3: Analyzing Alternatives
keyPoints: Involving others in generating alternatives brings different perspectives from different life experiences
A mentor can suggest options a newer manager would not think of alone
Creativity means using imagination to combine existing knowledge in new ways, not just a natural gift
Letting the mind wander, rather than staying intensely focused, often produces creative inspiration
segments.altExplanation: Two separate habits improve the options a manager has to choose from. Talking to people multiplies perspectives, because everyone brings different experience. Creativity multiplies possibility, by recombining what a manager already knows in a way that has not been tried yet.
segments.deeper: The book treats creativity as a learnable skill rather than an innate talent, which matters for management: it means habits like stepping back from routine, viewing a problem from multiple angles, and searching for patterns can be taught and practiced. The passage promises more depth on creativity later in the book, in a later chapter.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does talking to other people help generate alternatives, according to the passage?
options: They bring different perspectives and experiences
Other people can implement the decision instead
Other people always know the fastest solution
Other people rarely disagree with a manager's first idea
checkpoint.answer: They bring different perspectives and experiences
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about other people bringing different perspectives or life experiences.

checkpoint.prompt: What does the passage mean when it says creativity is a skill you can develop, not just a natural trait?
checkpoint.answer: It means creativity comes from deliberate habits, such as letting your mind wander, combining existing knowledge in new ways, viewing a problem from multiple perspectives, and searching for patterns, rather than being something only naturally creative people can do.
checkpoint.rubric: Must say creativity can be practiced or developed through habits such as letting the mind wander, recombining existing knowledge, or viewing a problem from multiple angles, not that it is purely innate.

segments.title: Evidence-based decision-making
segments.script: When implementing Step 3, it is important to take many factors into consideration. Some alternatives might be more expensive than others, for example, and that information is often essential when analyzing options. Effective managers will ensure that they have collected sufficient information to assess the quality of the various options. They will also utilize the tactics described below: engaging in evidence-based decision-making, thinking critically, talking to other people, and considering long-term and ethical implications. Do you have the best-quality data and evidence? Evidence-based decision-making is an approach to decision-making that states that managers should systematically collect the best evidence available to help them make effective decisions. The evidence that is collected might include the decision maker's own expertise, but it is also likely to include external evidence, such as a consideration of other stakeholders, contextual factors relevant to the organization, potential costs and benefits, and other relevant information. With evidence-based decision-making, managers are encouraged to rely on data and information rather than their intuition. This can be particularly beneficial for new managers or for experienced managers who are starting something new. (Consider all the research that Rubio and Korey conducted while starting Away).
keyPoints: Step 3, analyzing alternatives, requires collecting sufficient information, such as on cost
Evidence-based decision-making means systematically collecting the best available evidence rather than relying on intuition
Evidence includes the decision maker's own expertise as well as external evidence, like stakeholders, costs and benefits
This approach is especially useful for new managers, or experienced managers trying something new
segments.altExplanation: Evidence-based decision-making is a discipline: instead of trusting a gut feeling, a manager deliberately gathers expertise, stakeholder input, and cost information before deciding. It does not replace judgment, but it gives that judgment something solid to stand on.
segments.deeper: This ties back to the barriers to good decision-making covered earlier in the chapter, particularly bounded rationality and time constraints: gathering good evidence takes real effort, which is exactly the effort that pressure or a shortage of time tends to squeeze out. Evidence-based decision-making is the discipline of protecting that effort in Step 3 of the process.

checkpoint.prompt: What is evidence-based decision-making, and why can it especially help a new manager?
checkpoint.answer: It is an approach where managers systematically collect the best available evidence, such as their own expertise, stakeholder input, and cost-benefit information, rather than relying mainly on intuition. It especially helps new managers, or experienced managers trying something new, because they have less built-up intuition or experience with the situation to rely on.
checkpoint.rubric: Must describe systematically collecting evidence, such as expertise plus external evidence like stakeholders or costs, instead of relying on intuition, and explain that it helps managers with less relevant experience.

checkpoint.prompt: In Step 3 of the decision-making process, what should effective managers make sure they have collected?
options: A single alternative to avoid confusion
Sufficient information to assess the quality of the options
Signatures from every stakeholder before proceeding
Approval from senior management first
checkpoint.answer: Sufficient information to assess the quality of the options
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about collecting sufficient information to assess the quality of the alternatives.

segments.title: Talking to others and thinking critically
segments.script: As mentioned previously, it can be worthwhile to get help from others when generating options. Another good time to talk to other people is while analyzing those options; other individuals in the organization may help you assess the quality of your choices. Seeking out the opinions and preferences of others is also a great way to maintain perspective, so getting others involved can help you to be less biased in your decision-making (provided you talk to people whose biases are different from your own). Are you thinking critically about the options? Our skill at assessing alternatives can also be improved by a focus on critical thinking. Critical thinking is a disciplined process of evaluating the quality of information, especially data collected from other sources and arguments made by other people, to determine whether the source should be trusted or whether the argument is valid. An important factor in critical thinking is the recognition that a person's analysis of the available information may be flawed by a number of logical fallacies that they may use when they are arguing their point or defending their perspective. Learning what those fallacies are and being able to recognize them when they occur can help improve decision-making quality.
keyPoints: Talking to others while analyzing alternatives helps assess their quality and reduces bias, especially when their biases differ from your own
Critical thinking means disciplined evaluation of the quality of information and arguments, to judge whether a source can be trusted
Recognizing logical fallacies people use when arguing for a position is an important part of thinking critically
segments.altExplanation: Analyzing alternatives is not something to do alone. Other people help test the strength of your options, and critical thinking helps you test the strength of the information and arguments behind them, including catching flawed reasoning.
segments.deeper: This connects to the biases covered earlier in the chapter: talking to people whose biases differ from your own is one direct way to counter similar-to-me and confirmation bias while analyzing alternatives. Critical thinking, applied here to arguments and evidence, is the discipline that catches the logical fallacies people fall back on when defending a position.

checkpoint.prompt: Which of these is critical thinking, as the passage describes it?
options: Favoring people who share your background
Choosing the first acceptable option to save time
Judging whether information can be trusted
Staying committed to a decision already invested in
checkpoint.answer: Judging whether information can be trusted
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about evaluating whether information and arguments should be trusted.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the passage recommend talking to people whose biases differ from your own when analyzing alternatives?
checkpoint.answer: Because seeking out opinions and preferences different from your own helps you maintain perspective and be less biased in your decision-making.
checkpoint.rubric: Must say that talking to people with different biases or perspectives helps reduce bias or maintain perspective when assessing alternatives.

segments.title: Weighing long-term and ethical implications
segments.script: Have you considered the long-term implications? A focus on immediate, short-term outcomes, with little consideration for the future, can cause problems. For example, imagine that a manager must decide whether to issue dividends to investors or put that money into research and development to maintain a pipeline of innovative products. It's tempting to just focus on the short-term: providing dividends to investors tends to be good for stock prices. But failing to invest in research and development might mean that in five years the company is unable to compete effectively in the marketplace, and as a result the business closes. Paying attention to the possible long-term outcomes is a crucial part of analyzing alternatives. Are there ethical implications? It's important to think about whether the various alternatives available to you are better or worse from an ethical perspective, as well. Sometimes managers make unethical choices because they haven't considered the ethical implications of their actions. In the 1970s, Ford manufactured the Pinto, which had an unfortunate flaw: the car would easily burst into flames when rear-ended. The company did not initially recall the vehicle because they viewed the problem from a financial perspective, without considering the ethical implications. People died as a result of the company's inaction. Unfortunately, these unethical decisions continue to occur, and cause harm, on a regular basis in our society. Effective managers strive to avoid these situations by thinking through the possible ethical implications of their decisions. The decision tree is a great example of a way to make managerial decisions while also taking ethical issues into account.
keyPoints: Focusing only on short-term outcomes, like paying dividends instead of investing in research and development, can hurt a company later
Managers sometimes make unethical choices simply because they never considered the ethical angle
Ford's decision on the Pinto shows how viewing a problem only financially, without ethics, can cause real harm
Effective managers deliberately think through possible ethical implications before deciding
segments.altExplanation: Two extra questions belong alongside evidence and critical thinking when analyzing alternatives: what happens years from now, and who could be harmed. The Pinto example shows what happens when a company answers only the short-term, financial question and skips the ethical one entirely.
segments.deeper: The dividends-versus-research-and-development choice is a classic tension in management between short-term shareholder returns and long-term competitiveness. The Ford Pinto case is a well-known example in business ethics of a company treating a safety defect as a cost-benefit calculation rather than a moral question, used here to show that ethical blindness is often a failure to even ask the ethical question, not a decision to do wrong.

checkpoint.prompt: Why did Ford not initially recall the Pinto, according to the passage?
options: It could not identify what had caused the flaw
Its engineers concluded the flaw did not exist
Regulators had not yet required a recall
It viewed the problem only from a financial perspective
checkpoint.answer: It viewed the problem only from a financial perspective
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about viewing the problem only from a financial perspective, without considering ethics.

checkpoint.prompt: What example does the passage give of weighing short-term versus long-term outcomes, and what is the risk of focusing only on the short term?
checkpoint.answer: A manager choosing to pay dividends to investors instead of investing in research and development. Focusing only on the short-term stock-price benefit risks leaving the company unable to compete in five years and possibly closing.
checkpoint.rubric: Must reference the dividends-versus-research-and-development example and state the long-term risk, such as losing competitiveness, from ignoring the future.

segments.title: The four steps of ethical decision-making
segments.script: Moral sensitivity, recognizing that the issue has a moral component; Moral judgment, determining which actions are right versus wrong; Moral motivation or intention, deciding to do the right thing; and Moral character or action, actually doing what is right. Note that a failure at any point in the chain can lead to unethical actions! Taking the time to identify possible ethical implications will help you develop moral sensitivity, which is a critical first step to ensuring that you are making ethical decisions. Once you have determined that a decision has ethical implications, you must consider whether your various alternatives are right or wrong, whether or not they will cause harm, and if so, how much and to whom. This is the moral judgment component. If you aren't sure about whether something is right or wrong, think about how you would feel if that decision ended up on the front page of a major newspaper. If you would feel guilty or ashamed, don't do it! Pay attention to those emotional cues, they are providing important information about the option that you are contemplating. The third step in the ethical decision-making model involves making a decision to do what is right, and the fourth step involves following through on that decision. These may sound, but consider a situation in which your boss tells you to do something that you know to be wrong. When you push back, your boss makes it clear that you will lose your job if you don't do what you've been told to do. Now, consider that you have family at home who rely on your income. Making the decision to do what you know is right could come at a substantial cost to you personally. In these situations, your best course of action is to find a way to persuade your boss that the unethical action will cause greater harm to the organization in the long-term.
keyPoints: The four steps are moral sensitivity, moral judgment, moral motivation, and moral character or action
A failure at any one of the four steps can lead to an unethical outcome
Judging right from wrong means asking whether and how much harm an option would cause, and imagining how it would look publicly
Following through on doing what is right can carry a real personal cost, such as risking your job
segments.altExplanation: Recognizing that a decision has an ethical side is only the first step; judging what is right, actually intending to do it, and then following through are three more separate hurdles. The chapter's boss-pressure example shows how the last hurdle, actually acting, can be the hardest one.
segments.deeper: This four-step model, moral sensitivity, moral judgment, moral motivation, and moral character, is a widely used framework in business ethics for explaining why good values do not always translate into ethical action: a person can recognize and judge a situation correctly and still fail to act on it under pressure, which is exactly the boss scenario the passage describes.

checkpoint.prompt: What are the four steps involved in ethical decision-making?
checkpoint.answer: The four steps are moral sensitivity, recognizing that an issue has a moral component; moral judgment, determining which actions are right or wrong; moral motivation, deciding to do the right thing; and moral character, actually doing what is right.
checkpoint.rubric: Must name at least three of the four steps in substance: recognizing the moral issue, judging right from wrong, deciding or intending to do right, and actually acting on it.

checkpoint.prompt: In the passage's example, what makes it hard to follow through on step four when a boss pressures you to do something wrong?
options: It could come at a real personal cost
The situation has not been recognized as a decision yet
The moral judgment step has not yet been completed
You have not generated enough alternatives to choose from
checkpoint.answer: It could come at a real personal cost
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about a real personal cost, such as losing your job.

segments.title: Selecting an alternative
segments.script: Step 4: Selecting an Alternative Once alternative options have been generated and analyzed, the decision maker must select one of the options. Sometimes this is easy, one option is clearly superior to the others. Often, however, this is a challenge because there is not a clear "winner" in terms of the best alternative. As mentioned earlier in the chapter, there may be multiple good options, and which one will be best is unclear even after gathering all available evidence. There may not be a single option that doesn't upset some stakeholder group, so you will make someone unhappy no matter what you choose. A weak decision maker may become paralyzed in this situation, unable to select among the various alternatives for lack of a clearly "best" option. They may decide to keep gathering additional information in hopes of making their decision easier. As a manager, it's important to think about whether the benefit of gathering additional information will outweigh the cost of waiting. If there are time pressures, waiting may not be possible. Effective managers recognize that they will not always make optimal (best possible) decisions because they don't have complete information and/or don't have the time or resources to gather and process all the possible information. They accept that their decision-making will not be perfect and strive to make good decisions overall. Recognizing that perfection is impossible will also help managers to adjust and change if they realize later on that the selected alternative was not the best option. This is another point in the process at which talking to others can be helpful. Selecting one of the alternatives will ultimately be your responsibility, but when faced with a difficult decision, talking through your choice with someone else may help you clarify that you are indeed making the best possible decision from among the available options. Sharing information verbally also causes our brains to process that information differently, which can provide new insights and bring greater clarity to our decision-making.
keyPoints: Selecting is easy when one option is clearly superior, but there is often no clear "winner"
A weak decision maker can become paralyzed, endlessly gathering more information instead of deciding
Managers should weigh whether more information is worth the cost of waiting, especially under time pressure
Accepting that perfection is unattainable, and talking a choice through with someone else, both help a manager still decide well
segments.altExplanation: Step 4 is where indecision becomes its own risk. When no option is obviously best, the danger is not picking the wrong one, it is never picking one at all, because more research always looks tempting. The passage's advice is to accept an imperfect decision and, if it helps, to talk it through with someone else first.
segments.deeper: This connects back to bounded rationality and time constraints from earlier in the chapter: even at the selection stage, managers cannot wait for perfect certainty, because the cost of waiting keeps rising. Talking a decision through with someone else here echoes the same practice used earlier in generating and analyzing alternatives, because verbalizing a decision forces the brain to process it differently.

checkpoint.prompt: What can happen to a weak decision maker when no alternative is a clear 'winner'?
options: They delegate the decision to a mentor
They become paralyzed and keep gathering more information
They abandon the decision-making process entirely
They automatically pick the cheapest option
checkpoint.answer: They become paralyzed and keep gathering more information
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about becoming paralyzed and continuing to gather information rather than deciding.

checkpoint.prompt: According to the passage, why does recognizing that perfection is unattainable help a manager make decisions?
checkpoint.answer: It helps managers accept that their decisions will not always be optimal because they lack complete information, time, or resources, so they can still strive to make good overall decisions and stay willing to adjust course later if a choice turns out not to be the best one.
checkpoint.rubric: Must say that accepting imperfection lets managers still decide despite incomplete information or time, and helps them adjust later if needed.

segments.title: Implementing and evaluating the decision
segments.script: Step 5: Implementing the Selected Alternative After selecting an alternative, you must implement it. This may seem too obvious to even mention, but implementation can sometimes be a challenge, particularly if the decision is going to create conflict or dissatisfaction among some stakeholders. Sometimes we know what we need to do but still try to avoid actually doing it because we know others in the organization will be upset, even if it's the best solution. Follow-through is a necessity, however, to be effective as a manager. If you are not willing to implement a decision, it's a good idea to engage in some self-reflection to understand why. If you know that the decision is going to create conflict, try to think about how you'll address that conflict in a productive way. It's also possible that we feel that there is no good alternative, or we are feeling pressured to make a decision that we know deep down is not right from an ethical perspective. These can be among the most difficult of decisions. You should always strive to make decisions that you feel good about, which means doing the right thing, even in the face of pressures to do wrong. Step 6: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Your Decision Managers sometimes skip the last step in the decision-making process because evaluating the effectiveness of a decision takes time, and managers, who are generally busy, may have already moved on to other projects. Yet evaluating effectiveness is important. When we fail to evaluate our own performance and the outcomes of our decisions, we cannot learn from the experience in a way that enables us to improve the quality of our future decisions. Attending fully to each step in the decision-making process improves the quality of decision-making and, as we've seen, managers can engage in a number of tactics to help them make good decisions. Take a look at the Ethics in Practice box to see an example of how one particular manager puts these techniques into practice to make good decisions.
keyPoints: Implementing a decision can be hard, especially when it creates conflict or dissatisfaction among stakeholders
Avoiding implementation of a decision you know is right, out of fear of upsetting others, is a failure of follow-through
Step 6, evaluating effectiveness, is often skipped because managers are busy and have moved on
Without evaluating outcomes, managers cannot learn from experience to improve future decisions
segments.altExplanation: Choosing well is not the end of the process. A manager who avoids acting on a hard decision, or never checks how it turned out, has left the job half done. Both steps take a kind of discipline that is easy to skip once a decision feels settled.
segments.deeper: This closes the loop on the six-step process introduced earlier in the section: deciding well only pays off if the decision is actually carried out and its outcome is honestly evaluated. The passage frames follow-through as an ethical matter too, doing what you know is right even when it creates conflict, which links back to the personal-cost example from the ethical decision-making steps.

checkpoint.prompt: Why do managers sometimes skip Step 6, evaluating the effectiveness of a decision, and why does the passage say this matters?
checkpoint.answer: Managers skip it because evaluating effectiveness takes time and busy managers have often already moved on to other projects. It matters because without evaluating the outcome, managers cannot learn from the experience in a way that improves the quality of their future decisions.
checkpoint.rubric: Must give the reason, such as busy managers moving on, and the cost, such as failing to learn from the outcome to improve future decisions.

checkpoint.prompt: According to the passage, why might a manager avoid implementing a decision they know is right?
options: They have not talked the decision through with anyone
They have not yet evaluated its long-term effectiveness
They know it will create conflict or upset some stakeholders
They are still generating additional alternatives
checkpoint.answer: They know it will create conflict or upset some stakeholders
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about knowing the decision will create conflict or upset stakeholders.

segments.title: Rob Ault on ethical dilemmas
segments.script: Rob Ault, Project Manager, Bayside Community Church Bradenton, Florida When it comes to decision-making, ethical dilemmas require particular care. Because managers make many decisions, it should not be surprising that some of those decisions will have ethical implications. With multiple stakeholders to consider, sometimes what is best for one group of stakeholders is not what is best for others. I talked to Rob Ault about his experiences with ethical dilemmas over the course of his career. Rob has been in managerial roles for over 25 years, since he was 19 years old. He told me that he had experienced a number of ethical dilemmas in that time. Rob has spent most of his career working for for-profit organizations, and for about half of that time he has worked in a union environment. What he has found most frustrating, regardless of environment, was when it was clear to him what was right, but what was right conflicted with what his boss was telling him to do. This included a situation in which he felt an employee should be fired for misbehavior (but wasn't), as well as situation in which he was asked to fire someone undeservedly. What we mostly talked about, though, was his process. How did he go about making decisions in these challenging situations? Rob clearly stated that his approach to these situations has changed with experience. What he did early in his career is not necessarily what he would do now. He said that it takes experience and some maturity to recognize that, as a leader, the decisions you make affect other people's lives. He also explained that a starting point for the decision-making process is always a recognition of the fact that you have been hired to generate a benefit for your company. So a manager's decisions need to come from the perspective of what is going to be in the best long-term interest of the organization (in addition to what is morally right). This isn't always easy, because short-term consequences are much easier to observe and predict.
keyPoints: Rob Ault has worked in managerial roles for over 25 years, in both for-profit and union environments
What frustrated him most was when what he knew was right conflicted with what his boss told him to do
His approach to ethical dilemmas has changed with experience and maturity over his career
He starts from recognizing he was hired to benefit the company, alongside doing what is morally right
segments.altExplanation: The Ethics in Practice profile puts the chapter's ideas into one manager's real experience. Rob Ault names the exact tension the four-step model describes, knowing what is right and having a boss push the opposite way, and says that handling it well came with experience, not from day one.
segments.deeper: Rob Ault's framing, that a manager's decisions need to serve the organization's long-term interest as well as what is morally right, echoes the chapter's earlier point about weighing long-term implications: short-term consequences are easy to see, which is exactly why they can crowd out the ethical and long-term view.

checkpoint.prompt: What did Rob Ault find most frustrating in his managerial career, according to the passage?
options: When he had too many alternatives to choose from
When customers complained about product quality
When he lacked enough evidence to decide quickly
When what was right conflicted with his boss
checkpoint.answer: When what was right conflicted with his boss
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about what was right conflicting with what his boss told him to do.

checkpoint.prompt: According to Rob Ault, what should a manager's decisions be based on?
checkpoint.answer: What is going to be in the best long-term interest of the organization, in addition to what is morally right.
checkpoint.rubric: Must include both the organization's long-term interest and moral rightness; naming only one is partial.

segments.title: Building a network before hard decisions
segments.script: I asked Rob who he talked to prior to making decisions in situations with an ethical component. Rob told me that he felt one of the most important things you should do as a leader is to intentionally create and build relationships with people you trust in the organization. That way you have people you know you can talk to when difficult situations come up. He was very clear that you should always talk to your boss, who will tend to have a broader understanding of what is going on in the context of the larger organization. He also told me that he liked to talk to his father, who happened to work in human resource management for a large Fortune 500 organization. His father was always helpful in providing the perspective of how things were likely to play out long-term if one person was allowed to bend the rules. Rob realized eventually that the long-term consequences of this were almost always negative: once one person is allowed to misbehave, others find out about it and realize that they can do the same thing without repercussions. Rob also seeks out the opinions of other individuals in the organization before reaching decisions with an ethical component; he told me that when he worked in a union environment, he tried to make sure he had a good relationship with the union steward, because it was helpful to get the perspective of someone who was committed to the side of the employee. The biggest ethical dilemma Rob faced was one that he actually couldn't talk to me about. He disagreed with what he was being asked to do, and when it was clear that he had no other choice in the matter, he quit his job rather than do something he felt wasn't right. He accepted a severance package in exchange for signing a nondisclosure agreement, which is why he can't share any details... but it was clear from our conversation that he feels he made the right choice. That particular ethical dilemma makes it clear how challenging managerial decision-making can sometimes be.
keyPoints: Rob Ault built relationships with trusted people in the organization in advance, so he had people to talk to when it mattered
He always talked to his boss, and also to his father, who worked in human resource management at a large company
Tolerating one person's misbehavior teaches others they can do the same, so problems compound over time
His hardest ethical dilemma led him to quit his job rather than do something he felt was wrong
segments.altExplanation: Rob Ault's practice was to build trusted relationships before he needed them, not scramble for advice in the moment. When his hardest dilemma left him no other choice, he was willing to leave the job entirely rather than act against his values.
segments.deeper: This is a real-world instance of the chapter's advice to talk to other people while making a decision, extended into a habit: cultivating relationships in advance so good counsel is available under pressure. It also illustrates the broader theme that inaction is itself a consequential decision, since tolerating one person's rule-bending compounds over time as others copy it.

checkpoint.prompt: Why did Rob Ault say it was important to build relationships with trusted people in the organization in advance?
checkpoint.answer: So that he would already have people he knew he could talk to whenever a difficult or ethically challenging situation came up.
checkpoint.rubric: Must say the point was having trusted people to talk to before or when difficult situations arise, not just talking to people in general.

checkpoint.prompt: What did Rob Ault ultimately do when he felt he had no other ethical choice in his biggest dilemma?
options: He quit his job rather than do wrong
He asked the union steward to intervene
He reported the issue directly to a regulator
He delayed the decision until he retired
checkpoint.answer: He quit his job rather than do wrong
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about quitting his job rather than doing what he felt was wrong.
